author: Grace Chen
title: Michigan Wildlife Rehab Needs Your Help | Increased Animal Cases
text:
Northern Michigan Wildlife Center Overwhelmed as Human-Animal Interactions Surge As tourism increases in the region, the Sleeping Bear Wildlife Fund is working tirelessly to care for a growing number of injured and orphaned animals.
Benzie County , Mich. – With summer bringing increased visitation to northern Michigan, encounters between people and wildlife are on the rise, placing a significant strain on local rehabilitation efforts. The Sleeping Bear Wildlife Fund , established in 2021, is at the forefront of responding to this surge in need, providing critical care for injured and orphaned native animals.
A Lifelong Passion Drives Wildlife Rescue The center was co-founded by Samantha Wolfe , a lifelong advocate for wildlife. “You know I follow my passions and they don’t always lead to where the money is,” Wolfe stated, emphasizing her dedication to animal welfare . Recognizing a gap in local resources, she established the Benzie County rehabilitation center to address the growing need for specialized care.
Currently, the center is providing sanctuary for 32 animals, a diverse group including 17 opossums, seven squirrels , one weasel, one porcupine, and six foxes. The facility operates with the full approval of the Michigan Department of Natural Resources (DNR), appearing on their list of permitted rehabbers within the state.
Comprehensive Care: From Rescue to Release The Sleeping Bear Wildlife Fund offers a holistic approach to animal rehabilitation. “We will help out, whether it’s taking the animal in, rehabilitating it and re-releasing it into the wild, figuring out what the best course of action is for that particular animal or helping them figure out a way to coexist with it in their backyard,” Wolfe explained. This commitment extends beyond immediate medical attention to encompass long-term solutions for both animal welfare and human-wildlife coexistence.
The increased influx of visitors is directly contributing to the center’s heightened workload. “There are a lot more interactions with wildlife and particularly in the summer,” Wolfe noted. “We see it with everyone here from coming up north. They give us a call because they’re staying at a rental maybe and there’s something going on with an animal in their yard.”
Protecting Vulnerable Species, Like Turtles Wolfe also highlighted a specific seasonal concern: the safety of turtles attempting to cross roadways to reach nesting habitats. “They just are trying to get to the best habitat to lay those eggs and sometimes there’s a road in the way,” she said, urging caution from drivers and residents.
The Importance of Professional Wildlife Assistance In an era of readily available online information, Wolfe strongly advises against self-diagnosis or treatment. “Don’t rely on Dr. Google,” she cautioned. “If you find an animal look for a DNR licensed rehabber and they can help you out with actual science-based and experience-based knowledge.” This emphasis on professional expertise underscores the complexity of wildlife care and the potential for harm caused by well-intentioned but unqualified intervention.
A Nonprofit Reliant on Community Support The Sleeping Bear Wildlife Fund operates as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, relying on a combination of grants, donations, and in-kind contributions. “We take donations when people bring animals in. We often receive checks from people who have heard about us and then we apply for a lot of grants,” Wolfe explained.
Currently, the center is facing a critical shortage of essential supplies, including cleaning products, paper towels, and nitrile gloves. The cost of feeding the animals, particularly the six foxes and one weasel, is substantial. “With six foxes and a weasel to feed, they all eat whole prey every day. And so that adds up to more than $50 a meal per day,” Wolfe noted. The center is actively seeking donations of leftover venison or other suitable whole prey items from local hunters and residents.
Preserving Michigan’s Natural Heritage Wolfe’s dedication stems from a deep appreciation for the region’s natural beauty and biodiversity. “I really love this area and I think an important part of it is the wildlife and the landscapes that make it up,” she said.
For individuals outside of Benzie County seeking assistance, a network of licensed and regulated rehabilitation centers exists throughout the state. Further information, including contact details, resources, and donation opportunities for the Sleeping Bear Wildlife Fund, can be found on their website.
Wildlife Encounters: What You Can Do As the Sleeping Bear Wildlife Fund continues its vital work assisting injured and orphaned animals, it’s important to consider the role we all play in minimizing negative interactions with wildlife. Increased tourism in northern Michigan, as highlighted earlier, directly correlates with a rise in human-animal encounters. This demands both proactive measures and a shift in perspective, emphasizing the shared responsibility for protecting our natural heritage. Understanding the common causes of these encounters and implementing preventative actions can significantly reduce the strain on wildlife rehabilitation centers and,more importantly,protect the animals themselves.
Many issues arise due to unintentional actions. for example, improperly stored food attracts animals like raccoons, bears, and skunks.Feeding wildlife,whether intentionally or unintentionally,disrupts their natural foraging behaviour and can lead to dependence on humans. Habitat loss is another major issue. As human growth expands,wildlife habitat shrinks,forcing animals into closer proximity with people. This increased interaction inevitably leads to conflict.
Beyond these habitat and behavioral shifts, there are also significant dangers from cars, as Wolfe pointed out with turtles. roads can pose a significant threat during migration and nesting seasons. Moreover, domestic animals, such as cats and dogs, can also negatively impact wildlife through predation and disturbance. Simple steps taken by residents and visitors alike can help make a difference.
How to Be Wildlife-Pleasant Residents and visitors can minimize negative interactions and support wildlife conservation efforts. Here are some actionable steps:
Secure Food Sources: Store all food, including pet food and birdseed, in airtight containers. Keep trash cans securely closed or in a shed or garage. Never Feed Wildlife: This includes intentionally leaving food out or inadvertently creating food sources, such as unkempt bird feeders. Protect Pets: Keep cats indoors or supervised outdoors. Leash dogs when walking in areas frequented by wildlife. Drive Carefully: Pay attention to speed limits and posted wildlife crossing signs while driving,especially at dawn and dusk. Support Local Efforts: Donate to organizations like the Sleeping Bear Wildlife Fund and other local wildlife rehabilitation centers. Educate Yourself: Learn about the local wildlife and their behaviors to better understand how to coexist. Report Concerns: If you observe sick, injured, or orphaned wildlife, contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator, such as those listed on the Michigan DNR website. By adhering to these guidelines, the local community and visitors improve the chances of coexisting peacefully with wildlife. Remember, our actions have consequences, and we all benefit from a healthy and thriving ecosystem.
Spotlighting a Success Story While challenges abound, there are also encouraging examples of triumphant co-existence and conservation efforts. One such case involves a local effort to create safe passage for a specific group of turtles. By strategically placing signs and utilizing education campaigns, drivers began altering their behavior. This resulted in a noticeable decrease in road mortality for that particular species, demonstrating the effectiveness of focused, community-driven initiatives. These positive outcomes require commitment and collaboration between organizations like the Sleeping Bear Wildlife Fund, local government, and individual citizens.
Do you no what constitutes a wild animal emergency? If you find an animal that is obviously injured, orphaned, or showing signs of illness, contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. They can assess the situation and provide specialized care, as emphasized by Wolfe. Is it safe to handle a wild animal? Absolutely not. Wild animals can inflict injury and may transmit diseases. It’s best to observe from a distance and seek professional help.
Addressing the increasing rate of contact between humans and wildlife requires proactive, community-based solutions. These steps, when paired with resources like the Sleeping Bear Wildlife Fund, provide a framework for safeguarding our shared natural heritage and fostering a more harmonious relationship with the diverse animal populations of northern Michigan. The commitment to wildlife care,fueled by passion and community support,becomes central to maintaining the beauty and biodiversity that makes the area such a special place to visit and call home.
